key_specs: ALREADY IN THE LAB - listed so a replicator can buy one. Hydrophobic PTFE membrane in a PP housing, 0.2 um, 50 mm disc, 16.2 cm2 effective area, supplied sterile. Stepped hose barb for 1/4 to 3/8 in (6-9.5 mm) ID tubing, so it needs a step down to the 4 mm line the riser takes. Area-correcting Pall Acro 50 to 16.2 cm2 gives 3.02, so the figure used is 14 % conservative of the best-documented comparable part. key_specs: ROD SEAL, and the only one in the build that is: the sparger riser passes up the bore of its port and this closes the annulus around it. Two of them, one in air_in and one in air_out, sitting in a counterbore at the lid's INNER face so headspace pressure drives the cord onto the shoulder rather than out past it. WHAT IT IS FOR: without it each gas port is a 2.64 mm2 hole into the headspace against a 7.07 mm2 intended vent, so most of the exhaust left by the gap and the inlet sterile filter guarded a vessel that was open to the room. key_specs: STOCK LENGTH, cut to make two tubes: the sparger feed riser and its support tube, 186.637 mm each as drawn - 14.9375 mm proud of the port for a hose clamp, down to 8 mm inside the socket. 373.275 mm total, so the model asks for a 500 mm length; buying the 1 m at 22.72 rather than the 0.5 m at 13.28 leaves 626 mm spare - enough to remake both twice and to feed the bent-tube sparger variant in TODO. WELDED, not seamless: at 4 mm OD the seamless equivalent is 181.42/m against 22.72, is SOFT temper where a support tube wants hard, and comes only in a 1 mm wall so a 2 mm bore. The weld bead costs nothing here - the riser drops a few hundred Pa against the 24 kPa the metering valve burns, and the support tube is a dead leg by design, which is a worse crevice than a bead either way. 4 x 2.5 mm, which this row used to name, is not a size anyone sells. 316 because it is wetted and stays in the culture. The support one is capped at the ring and takes a drilled hole or filed slit at whatever height its own job wants. Deburr the ID after cutting - a wheel cutter rolls a 0.5 mm wall inward.

brand_model: Dwyer VFA-23 acrylic variable-area flow meter, 0.6-5 L/min air, no valve
key_specs: Closes the measured-gas-flow gap. 0.1-0.5 vvm on 8.25 L is 0.825-4.125 L/min, so the design point sits at 82.5% of a 5 L/min scale and 0.1 vvm at 16.5% - both on scale, which is what a 0-5 range buys. THE SCALE READS L/MIN, and only one other candidate did: everything McMaster sells in this range reads scfh, where the design point is 8.66 of them and every reading in the paper carries a conversion. CALIBRATION BASIS IS THE SPEC THAT DECIDED IT - Dwyer bulletin F-33 gives 14.7 psia and 70 F, which is this regime, so the correction at the line back-pressure is 0.7%. The medical channel is referenced at 50 psig and the welding channel at 30, which would read 87% wrong here, and that ruled both out entirely rather than on price. Accuracy is 5% of FULL SCALE, so 0.25 L/min, which is 6.1% at the design point; Cole-Parmer have no 5 L/min rung and their nearest tube is 8.5 full scale, costing 10.4% at the same point for 69% more money. THIS IS THE BARE METER. VFA-23-BV carries an integral brass valve whose Cv Dwyer do not publish, so the throttle is a separate characterised part instead - see the metering valve row - and that valve goes UPSTREAM of this meter, which is what the 0.7% correction assumes. Nickel-plated brass body, acrylic block, 1/8 NPT female back or end connection, so it needs NPT-to-barb adapters at both ends. Graduation interval is not published anywhere; over a 70 mm scale it resolves finer than the 0.25 L/min accuracy, so it is worth asking Dwyer but does not block ordering. Price is CAD 86.22 and the unit_price_usd column carries it unconverted, same as the filter row. See docs/procurement.md for the rejected candidates and what ruled each out.

brand_model: Clippard MNV-3KP miniature needle valve, 3 degree needle, knurled knob, #10-32 ports
key_specs: The throttle, and it sits UPSTREAM of the rotameter so the meter sees only downstream line loss. Required Cv is 0.0333 at the 4.125 L/min design point: the pump settles at 6.05 L/min against this line, so the valve drops 7.88 kPa on top of the line's own 17.41 - which now counts the check valve, so this figure moved once the line was fully accounted. WAS MNV-4K2 AND THE NEEDLE IS WHY IT IS NOT. Both carry the same capacity - Clippard rate each at 5 scfm at 100 psig, which back-solves to Cv 0.094 and confirms the 0.090 in the notes - so both put the design point at about 35% of wide open, 2.8x the required Cv. What differs is the taper: MNV-4 is a 20 degree needle, the COARSEST of the four and coarser than the MNV-1 this project had already rejected as too coarse, while MNV-3 is 3 degrees. Same capacity, same price bracket, roughly seven times the travel for the same flow change. That matters because the pump is seven times oversized, so the whole 0.83-4.13 L/min band is set in the first part of the valve travel. MNV-4K2 was picked on Cv alone without reading the needle diagram. The cost of switching is that MNV-3 has no barbed variant - it is #10-32 both ends and takes two 11792-4-BLK fittings - and adapters were being bought for the rotameter regardless. See docs/procurement.md for how the required Cv moved and what it retired, and the Clippard needle valve catalogue for the taper.

brand_model: Cole-Parmer miniature check valve, polypropylene body, Viton diaphragm, 3/16 in barb
key_specs: Stops culture siphoning back into the pump when it stops. Sits between the metering valve and the sterile filter. 0.18 psi cracking / 0.014 psi closing, published; Cv 0.12. REAL COST TO THE LINE IS 1.85 kPa - 1.24 of cracking plus 0.61 of flowing drop at the 4.087 L/min design point. The flowing half is never on a spec sheet and is what separates otherwise-identical parts: an Air Logic umbrella at the same nominal cracking pressure costs 0.9 kPa more because its flow capacity is a quarter of this one. 3/16 in barb is +19 % stretch on 4 mm ID silicone airline. Barb size barely affects flow here - Cole-Parmer publish Cv per size and it only moves 0.11 to 0.13 across 1/8 to 5/16 - so the barb is chosen to fit the tube, not to chase pressure. CHOSEN ON PROCUREMENT, NOT PHYSICS: US Plastic 22577 is 1.78 kPa, a 4 % difference, which is inside the error on the filter figure that dominates the budget. Same supplier as the sterile filter 1594522 means one shipment, one account, one customs clearance into Canada. Viton rather than the nylon/silicone sibling 5011519: nylon is hygroscopic and swells in continuously humid air. CONFIRM BEFORE ORDERING: the page reads "Working Pressure 3-5 psi" while the pump dead-heads at 3.9 psi and the valve runs at about 2.2 psig in service, so it sits below that band normally and at it on dead-head. The 0.014 psi closing pressure argues it seals fine at low pressure, but the wording is ambiguous. See docs/procurement.md for the other candidates and why each was rejected.

brand_model: McMaster compact metal tube and conduit cutter, 1/8 to 7/8 in OD
key_specs: Cuts the 316 SS riser stock into 2 x 187 mm. RATED FOR STAINLESS, which is the filter that rules out most cheap tube cutters - many are copper and aluminium only. 1/8 to 7/8 in OD, so the 4 mm (0.157 in) tube sits just above the minimum. Steel cutting wheel, grooved rollers, 1.5 in swing radius, 2 5/8 in long. Replacement wheels sold separately. IT DOES NOT DEBURR. A wheel cutter rolls material inward at the cut and the riser bore is only 3 mm, with that restriction landing exactly where gas enters - so an inside deburring tool is a separate row and a required assembly step, not a nicety. Noga RC1000 (3-5.5 mm) is the only tool found whose range brackets a 3 mm bore. A jeweller''s saw in a mitre jig is the alternative worth considering: a wheel cutter always rolls a thin wall inward, a saw does not, which removes the problem at source rather than fixing it after. Listed REACH and RoHS non-compliant - irrelevant here, it is a bench tool and never enters the reactor, unlike the wetted parts this project does hold to those standards.

key_specs: Second step, onto the 1/8 in line the Clippard fittings take. Same family and reasoning as the 3/8-1/4 above.

key_specs: Three short bores upstream of the sterile filter: 3/8 in off the pump 10 mm outlet, 1/4 in between the two reducers, 1/8 in from the second reducer through the metering valve to the rotameter inlet. Specified by BORE rather than a part number, the same way the fasteners are specified by standard - it is a commodity and a catalogue code would be region-specific and perishable. PVC or polyurethane rather than silicone, because the barbed fittings this side are rated for firm 75A-80A line and nothing here is inside the sterile boundary. Lengths are bench layout, not design: keep them short, since 1/8 in bore costs about 240 Pa per half metre at 4.125 L/min.

brand_model: Platinum-cure silicone tubing, 3/16 in (4.8 mm) ID, autoclavable
key_specs: From the rotameter outlet through the check valve and the sterile filter to the sparge riser. SILICONE here and not upstream, because everything past the 0.2 um filter is inside the sterile boundary and has to survive whatever sterilises it. One bore for the whole run: native on the check valve 3/16 in barb, stretched 33% onto the filter 1/4 in step, and 0.76 mm loose over the 4 mm riser under a clamp. THE STRETCHED FILTER JOINTS ARE THE ONES TO WATCH - silicone creeps, and this is the sterile barrier. WHERE A LEAK MATTERS: the rotameter reads what passes IT, so a leak upstream of the meter only costs flow that is then dialled back in, while a leak downstream means the vessel gets less than the meter claims and every vvm figure in docs/agitation.md is wrong by that much. All four risky joints - check valve twice, filter twice - are downstream.

brand_model: McMaster-Carr worm-drive hose clamp, 316 stainless band and screw, 5/16 in band, SAE 4 (5.6-15.875 mm)
key_specs: Every barbed joint in the gas line, 14 of them: 2 on the 3/8 in run, 2 on the 1/4 in, 4 on the 1/8 in, 6 on the 3/16 in silicone. ONE SIZE COVERS THE WHOLE LINE - SAE 4 spans 5.6-15.875 mm and the next size in this band starts at 11, so nothing else is needed. BAND WIDTH IS NOT A PREFERENCE, AND THE MODEL NOW READS IT: this clamp is registered in scad/purchased/hose_clamps.scad and head.scad derives sparge_riser_proud from its 7.9375 mm band plus 3.5 mm of lead-in either side, giving 14.9375. It was a literal 15 justified against a band 'about 9 mm wide', which is one band with two numbers. The 1/2 in band would be 12.7 and leave 2.3 mm of lead-in in total. 316 rather than the 301/zinc, 301/410 or 301/305 builds of the same clamp: a plated screw rusts and seizes in the humid headspace the riser clamp sits in, and 305 and 316 are BOTH derated to 7.5 in-lbs, so 316 buys chloride margin on a chemically sterilised reactor at no torque cost - see procurement.md. THE TOP END IS THE EDGE CASE, NOT THE BOTTOM, AND IT IS EXACT: 3/8 in line in a 1/8 in wall is 15.875 mm and the SAE 4 stops at 15.875 - the same number twice, on a clamp at its last thread. Keep that run to 1/16 or 3/32 in wall (12.70 or 14.29 mm) or it alone wants an SAE 6. 316 on 316 galls, which is what the 7.5 in-lbs is about: snug them with the 1/4 in nut driver, never a wrench. Sold in tens, so 2 packs is the smallest buy that covers 14 joints.

brand_model: NOGA RC1000 mini reversible deburring tool, handle + blade
key_specs: For the sparge riser bore after cutting. The tube cutter row already flags this as a real assembly step rather than a nicety: a wheel cutter rolls a 0.5 mm wall INWARD, and on a 3 mm bore that restriction lands exactly where gas enters the ring. Reversible, so it deburrs the far side of a hole as well as the near one. NOT VERIFIED: the listing does not state the smallest bore its blade reaches, and 3 mm is at the small end of what a deburring blade will enter. Check blade reach before relying on it - a round needle file or a hand countersink does the same job on two cuts if it does not fit. CAD 41.00 on Amazon.ca.
